title: 6 Best Electric Pressure Washers (2026): Plug-In and Cordless
h1: The 6 Best Electric Pressure Washers in 2026
description: The Ryobi RY142300 brushless is the best electric pressure washer for most homes; 6 plug-in and cordless picks, all capped near 1,800 W by a 15-amp outlet.
dek: The Ryobi RY142300 brushless is the best electric pressure washer for most homes; 6 plug-in and cordless picks, all capped near 1,800 W by a 15-amp outlet.
intro: No fuel, no pull cord, no fumes. These plug-in and battery machines handle the jobs most homeowners actually do, and this guide is honest about the ones they cannot.

An electric pressure washer is the right tool for most homes, and the wrong one for a few. If your list is a car every month, a deck in spring, vinyl siding, a grill and some patio furniture, a good plug-in does all of it quietly and starts every time. If your list is dominated by a long concrete driveway, no electric will make that fast, because a household outlet caps how much water the pump can move. This guide ranks six electric machines, explains the motor and circuit limits that separate good ones from bad ones, and covers technique for the surfaces electric machines are best at.
quickAnswer: the Ryobi RY142300 2300 PSI Brushless is our #1 pick (top electric overall). The plug-in most households should buy for regular car, deck and siding work.

sections.h: What a Household Outlet Can Power

blocks.p: Every plug-in pressure washer is boxed in by the same constraint. A standard 120-volt, 15-amp circuit can safely supply about 1,800 watts continuously, and most machines are designed to draw 13 to 15 amps. That energy has to be split between pressure and flow. A pump can push a small amount of water at high pressure or more water at moderate pressure, but not a lot of both. That is why plug-ins top out around 1.1 to 1.8 GPM no matter how big the PSI number printed on the side is.

In practice, this means two electric machines with very different pressure ratings often clean at similar speeds. A 3,000 PSI unit at 1.1 GPM and a 2,000 PSI unit at 1.5 GPM deliver similar total cleaning energy, measured as pressure times flow. The higher-pressure machine is better at blasting a stubborn spot; the higher-flow machine is better at rinsing a big wall or a car. Choose based on which of those describes your work.
The Plug-In Envelope
Continuous limit, 15 A circuit
Typical GPM range
Typical rated PSI
Typical cleaning units

Pay attention to whether figures are labeled max or rated. Peak pressure is a spike the pump can reach briefly; peak flow is measured with no nozzle restriction. Real working figures are lower, sometimes considerably. Machines certified to the industry standards used by CETA or the PWMA publish rated performance you can compare more fairly. When a budget box lists only max numbers, treat them as optimistic and compare on price, motor and build instead.

Share the circuit with nothing else. Running a pressure washer on the same garage circuit as a freezer or a compressor invites nuisance trips and voltage drop that makes the motor work harder. If your outdoor outlet trips often under load, the machine is telling you something about the wiring, and that is a job for an electrician rather than a heavier extension cord.

The motor decides how loud the machine is and, often, how long it lasts. Universal motors, found on most budget plug-ins, spin very fast and use carbon brushes to carry current to the spinning armature. They are light and cheap, which is why they power most machines under about $200. They are also loud, run hot, and the brushes wear, so these machines tend to have shorter service lives, especially under long sessions.

Induction motors have no brushes and turn more slowly. They are heavier and cost more, but they run cooler, are noticeably quieter, and are commonly expected to last much longer. Machines like the Karcher K5 and the Greenworks Pro use them, and they are the better choice for anyone who washes regularly. Brushless DC motors, like the one in the Ryobi RY142300, get many of the same benefits with lighter weight and good efficiency.

Spec sheets do not always name the motor type. Clues include the weight, the price, and how the brand describes it: induction motors are usually advertised as such because they are a selling point, and brushless is always called out. A machine that weighs under 30 pounds, costs under $200 and says nothing about the motor almost certainly has a universal motor.

A universal motor is not a reason to avoid a machine if the jobs are short and occasional. A twenty-minute car wash once a month is well within what a budget unit can handle for years. It is a reason to avoid one if you plan to strip and wash a large deck or run the machine for hours at a time, where heat and brush wear accumulate.

Most manufacturers advise against extension cords or allow only short, heavy-gauge ones, and the reason is voltage drop. A long, thin cord starves the motor, which then draws more current, heats up and wears faster. If you must use one, check the manual and use the gauge it specifies, typically 12 or 14 gauge, kept as short as possible and fully unrolled. Keep connections off wet ground. The better approach is to put the machine near the outlet and run a longer high-pressure hose or garden hose instead.

Plug the machine into a GFCI-protected outlet. Electric pressure washers sold in the US come with a GFCI built into the plug, and you should press its test and reset buttons before each session. If the GFCI trips repeatedly, stop and look for a damaged cord or a water leak around the motor housing rather than resetting it again and again.

Water supply matters less with an electric than with gas, because flow demands are lower, but it still matters. Use a 5/8-inch garden hose of reasonable length with the spigot fully open, and make sure the inlet filter screen is clean. A kinked or undersized supply hose starves the pump, which shows up as pulsing pressure and a pump that cycles on and off.
Quick Check
Pulsing pressure is usually a supply problem.

Before blaming the pump, straighten the supply hose, open the spigot fully, clean the inlet screen, check for a partly blocked nozzle, and run water through the machine for a minute to purge trapped air.

The high-pressure hose that comes with budget electrics is often 20 to 25 feet of stiff plastic. Upgrading to a longer, more flexible hose with the correct fittings, frequently M22 threads on these machines, is one of the most useful changes you can make. Check the pressure rating of any replacement hose and confirm it matches or exceeds the machine's peak rating.

sections.h: What an Electric Cleans Well, and What It Does Not

blocks.p: Electric machines are at their best on surfaces that need moderate pressure and rinse easily: painted cars, trucks, bikes, outdoor furniture, plastic playsets, grills, vinyl and fiber cement siding, fences, and softwood decks. On all of these, a good electric is not a compromise. Many of these surfaces are damaged by too much pressure, so an electric is often the better tool than gas.

Concrete is where electrics struggle. Small areas such as steps, a front walk or a patio clean up fine, especially with an 11- to 15-inch surface cleaner rated for electric machines. A full two-car driveway is a different story. Expect it to take a long time, and expect stripes if you work with a wand alone. If concrete is a big part of your list, our broader [pressure washer rankings](/best-pressure-washer/) include gas machines built for that.

blocks.p: Oil stains, rust marks and deep mildew are chemistry problems, not pressure problems. A gas machine will not lift a set-in oil stain much better than an electric. Use a degreaser or poultice first; the methods in [getting oil out of concrete](/how-to-get-oil-out-of-concrete/) work regardless of which machine you rinse with afterward.

Roofs and stucco are jobs to skip with any pressure washer. Asphalt shingles lose granules under pressure, and stucco can absorb water and crack. Roof cleaning is normally done with a low-pressure chemical wash, and many homeowners hire it out. Old painted surfaces that may contain lead should not be blasted at all; use gentle washing methods and follow EPA guidance for older homes.

sections.h: Battery Pressure Washers: Where They Fit

blocks.p: Cordless pressure washers fall into two groups. The first is small spray guns that run on a power tool battery and draw water from a bucket or hose, delivering a few hundred PSI. They are useful for rinsing muddy bikes, boots, dog crates and car wheels, and they cost little if you already own the batteries. They are not substitutes for a real pressure washer.

The second group is full-size battery machines like the EGO model ranked above, which aim to match mid-range plug-ins. These are genuinely useful where outlets are not: a boat at a dock, a horse trailer, an RV at a campsite, the far side of a large property. The trade-off is runtime and cost. Large batteries are expensive, and continuous spraying drains them faster than lawn tools.

If you are buying a battery machine, buy it from a platform you already use. Batteries and chargers are often half the cost of a kit, and the value comes from sharing them with a mower, trimmer or blower. Our [Ryobi platform review](/ryobi-tools-review/) covers one ecosystem that includes several washer options, and the same logic applies to EGO, Greenworks and the professional tool brands.

For a house with an outdoor outlet and a hose bib, a corded machine remains the better value by a wide margin. Battery models make sense as a second machine or for specific remote jobs. They rarely make sense as the only pressure washer for someone who washes a house and deck every year.

sections.h: Technique for Cars, Decks and Siding

blocks.p: For a car, start with a rinse using the 40-degree tip held 18 to 24 inches from the paint. Apply foam or soap, let it dwell for a few minutes without drying in the sun, then hand wash with a mitt and rinse again from the top down. Keep the stream away from damaged paint chips, emblems, rubber seals and the edges of film or wraps. Never use the 0- or 15-degree tip on a vehicle.

For a wood deck, apply a deck cleaner suited to the problem, such as a percarbonate cleaner for gray, weathered wood, and let it work. Rinse with a 25- or 40-degree tip, keeping the wand about a foot from the surface and moving along the length of the boards with the grain. Fuzzy, raised fibers mean the pressure is too high or the tip too close. Let the deck dry for at least a couple of days before staining; our [deck stain guide](/best-deck-stain-reviews/) covers what to apply next.

For vinyl or fiber cement siding, apply detergent from the bottom up so streaks do not form on dry siding below, let it dwell, then rinse from the top down. Keep the stream level or angled down so water does not get pushed up behind the laps. Avoid spraying directly at window seals, vents, outlets and light fixtures. Use an extension wand for the upper story instead of working from a ladder.

For all three, start farther away than you think you need to and move closer only if the dirt is not lifting. Keep the wand moving and overlap passes. The goal is to let the detergent loosen the dirt and the water carry it away; pressure is the last thing you should increase, not the first.

Most electric machines pull detergent through an on-board tank or a siphon tube, and almost all of them only inject soap at low pressure. That is why you have to switch to the black soap tip or the low setting on an adjustable wand before soap will flow. If no soap is coming out, check that you are in low-pressure mode, that the tank is not empty, and that the screen on the pickup is not clogged.

Use detergents labeled for pressure washers. They are formulated to flow through the injector and rinse cleanly. Do not run bleach through the machine unless the manufacturer explicitly allows it, because chlorine can damage seals. Apply bleach-based solutions separately with a pump sprayer when cleaning mildew from siding or decks, and protect plants by wetting them before and after.

A foam cannon replaces the injector with a bottle that mixes soap, water and air into thick foam. For car washing it is the most useful accessory you can buy, because the foam clings and loosens grit before you touch the paint. It works on electric machines, though the foam is generally thinner than on gas units with more flow. Choose a cannon made for your machine's fitting and flow range.

Rinse the detergent system with clean water after each session. Dried soap blocks the injector and the pickup screen and is a common cause of no-soap complaints. A quick flush with a tank of plain water at the end of the job keeps it working for years.

Electric machines need less care than gas ones, but the pump is identical in its weaknesses. After each use, turn off the machine and the water, squeeze the trigger to release pressure, disconnect both hoses and let water drain out of the pump. Wipe the cord dry before coiling it. Store tips in their holder so the small orifices stay clean.

If the machine sits for more than a few weeks, or lives anywhere that could freeze, run a pump protector product through the inlet. These leave a lubricating, antifreeze film on seals and valves. A freeze can crack the pump head even on a small electric, and the damage often appears as a leak or no pressure when you next start it. Storing the machine inside a heated space over winter avoids the problem entirely.

Check the inlet filter screen periodically and rinse out any grit. Inspect the high-pressure hose for bulges or cuts and replace it if you see any. If quick connects drip, a fresh O-ring usually fixes them. Do not let the machine sit in bypass with the trigger released for more than a minute or two; electric pumps heat water quickly when it recirculates, and many shut off the motor automatically, but that heat still stresses the seals.

Most electric pressure washers carry warranties in the range of two to three years on the machine, sometimes with different terms for the pump. Register the product and keep the receipt. Many owners who report early pump failures turn out to have frozen or dry-run the machine, which warranties typically exclude.

At the time of writing, budget universal-motor electrics sell for roughly $120 to $220. Brushless and induction-motor machines sell for roughly $250 to $450. Full-size battery machines often land between $300 and $600 depending on how many batteries come in the box. Add $40 to $120 for a surface cleaner, foam cannon or better hose.

The extra money for a better motor pays back for anyone who washes regularly. A budget machine that wears out after a few seasons of heavy deck and siding work, then gets replaced, costs more over five years than a well-built machine bought once. If your use is a car and some furniture a few times a year, the budget machine is the smarter purchase and will likely last.

Compared with gas, an electric saves money in ways beyond the sticker. There is no fuel, no oil, no spark plugs, no stabilizer and no carburetor cleaning. For a household that washes a few times per month in warm weather, those running costs add up. The trade-off is speed on big concrete, which is why many homeowners pair an electric with an occasional rental for the driveway.

If you want to see how electrics compare against gas on cost and speed for every job, our full [pressure washer guide](/best-pressure-washer/) lays out both. If concrete is your main concern, a [surface cleaner](/best-surface-cleaner-for-pressure-washer/) is the accessory that makes an electric viable on patios and walks, and it is worth buying before you consider upgrading the machine.
Also Needed for This Job

mistakes: Running a Long, Thin Extension Cord

A 100-foot light-duty cord drops voltage enough to make the motor run hot and labor, which shortens its life and can trip the GFCI. Put the machine near the outlet and run more hose instead. If an extension is unavoidable, use the gauge and maximum length the manual allows and keep the connection off wet ground.
Trusting the Max PSI on the Box

Budget electrics publish peak numbers that are not reached during normal spraying. Comparing two machines on max PSI alone tells you little about how fast either will clean. Look for rated figures, multiply pressure by flow, and weigh the motor type and build quality, which tend to predict satisfaction better than a headline number.
Leaving the Trigger Released With the Motor On

Many electrics stop the motor when you release the trigger, but water in the pump still heats up if the machine sits in bypass. Long pauses with the machine running damage seals. If you are stopping to move furniture or reposition the hose, switch the machine off and release pressure first.
Using the Narrowest Tip on Soft Surfaces

Even an electric can splinter cedar, etch soft brick and peel paint with a 0- or 15-degree tip. Start with the 40-degree tip at a foot or more and only move closer or narrower if dirt is not lifting. Fuzzy wood fibers or exposed aggregate are signs you have already gone too far.

Owners often winterize the gas mower and forget the plug-in washer in the same shed. The pump holds water and cracks just as easily when it freezes. Drain it, run a pump protector through the inlet before cold weather, and store it somewhere above freezing whenever you can.
bottomLine: For most homes, the Ryobi RY142300 brushless is the electric to buy: quiet, durable, and compatible with standard accessories. If paint and finish matter most, the Karcher K5 Premium gives you the most control. For light chores on a budget, the Sun Joe SPX3000 and Westinghouse ePX3100 are fine, and the EGO battery model makes sense only if you already own its batteries or regularly clean away from outlets. Keep expectations matched to the outlet. An electric is excellent for cars, decks, siding and patios and slow on large concrete. Plug it into a GFCI outlet without a long cord, start with the widest tip, and protect the pump from freezing every fall.

faqs.q: Which electric pressure washer should most people buy?
faqs.a: For regular washing of cars, decks and siding, the Ryobi RY142300 brushless is the best all-round choice, with a quieter, longer-lived motor and standard fittings. For gentle, controlled work on paint, the Karcher K5 Premium is better. On a tight budget for light chores, the Sun Joe SPX3000 or Westinghouse ePX3100 do the job well.

faqs.q: Can an electric pressure washer clean a driveway?
faqs.a: It can, but slowly. Household outlets cap electric flow under about 2 GPM, so a full two-car driveway takes a long time and tends to stripe when cleaned with a wand. A surface cleaner sized for electric machines helps a lot on smaller areas. For large driveways cleaned every year, a gas machine or a rental is far more efficient.

faqs.q: Is a brushless or induction motor worth paying more for?
faqs.a: If you wash regularly, yes. Both run cooler and quieter than the universal motors in budget machines and are generally expected to last longer, since there are no carbon brushes to wear. For occasional short jobs, such as washing a car a few times a year, a budget universal-motor machine is usually adequate and will last for years.

faqs.q: Can I use an extension cord with an electric pressure washer?
faqs.a: Many manuals advise against it or allow only short, heavy-gauge cords, often 12 or 14 gauge. Long or thin cords cause voltage drop, which makes the motor overheat and can trip the GFCI. The better solution is to place the machine near the outlet and use a longer garden hose or high-pressure hose to reach the work.

faqs.q: How much pressure is safe on car paint?
faqs.a: Most car care guidance suggests staying around 1,200 to 1,900 PSI with a 40-degree tip held 18 to 24 inches from the paint. Pressure at the paint drops quickly with distance, so distance and tip angle matter as much as the rating. Avoid narrow tips entirely, and be careful around chips, trim, emblems and seals.

faqs.q: Are cordless pressure washers any good?
faqs.a: Small battery spray guns are handy for rinsing bikes, boots and wheels but are not real pressure washers. Full-size battery machines like EGO's are capable and useful where there is no outlet, such as at a dock or campsite. They are expensive unless you already own the batteries, so for most homes a corded electric is better value.

faqs.q: Why does my electric pressure washer keep turning on and off?
faqs.a: Short cycling usually means the pump is not getting steady water or air is trapped in the system. Open the spigot fully, straighten the supply hose, clean the inlet screen and nozzle, and run water through before starting the motor. If it persists, a worn unloader or a small leak in the gun or hose can cause the same symptom.
